newsitem.title: USA: Floodwaters, ice, and snow plague U.S. Plains.
newsitem.headline: Floodwaters, ice, and snow plague U.S. Plains.

text.p: Northern Plains states on Monday appealed for federal help after a powerful spring snowstorm blocked roads, knocked out power lines and swelled already overflowing rivers, leaving many homeless.
Only one death has been blamed on the destructive storm.
Volunteers and National Guard troops piled sandbags in frigid temperatures along rivers across the region as ice-coated tree limbs sagged dangerously overhead.

"You name it, we've got it. This is crazy," Capt. Pat Richards of North Dakota's Division of Emergency Management said, noting that scores of people had to be evacuated to shelters during the height of the weekend blizzard.
Thousands of people remained without power or heat and they were warned they would not have them back for days because scores of high-voltage power towers had collapsed.

Highways and many roads across North Dakota were blocked by downed power lines and littered with snowdrifts up to 10 feet (3 m) deep. Most schools were closed, and travel bans were in effect for all but essential trips in many towns.

The governors of North and South Dakota both asked for a presidential disaster declaration and Minnesota was preparing a request as the storm brought added misery to what was already shaping up as the flood of the century.

South Dakota was granted the disaster declaration and the other states were likely to gain approval of their requests. President Bill Clinton had granted federal aid a few months ago because of record snowfall, which has now begun melting.

"There's nothing like this historically," North Dakota State University geologist Donald Schwert said, taking a break from pumping out his flooded basement and clearing snowdrifts from around his Fargo home.

At the height of the storm, witnesses in Fargo reported seeing blue flashes from arcing electricity as transformers blew out. A television transmission tower was blown down by winds gusting to 70 miles per hour (113 kph).

In the only death attributed so far to the storm, a boy in Lisbon, North Dakota, died in a house fire sparked by candles that were lighted because the power had gone out. Telephones were also out and rescuers were hampered by snowy roads.

Hastily built dikes protecting Wahpeton, a city of 10,000 in the southeast corner of North Dakota, from the Red River became a threat when 3 inches (7.6 cm) of rain fell and nearly turned the town into a giant lake.
"We were almost drowning internally. The water couldn't escape because of the dikes," Mayor Dan Rood said. "So we had to pump that out, which we did feverishly."

The city rigged tractors to pump out the runoff when massive pumps being shipped from Minnesota were delayed by the storm. Wahpeton was also housing about 300 flooded-out residents from Breckenridge, a town across the Red River in Minnesota where dikes were overtopped.

In Minnesota, an evacuation order was issued on Monday for the 1,700 residents of Ada, where the Wild Rice River was swamping much of the town. Many vehicles were frozen in place as floodwaters turned to ice.

Huge ice chunks threatened dikes along the Minnesota River by the town of Montevideo where volunteers have spent the past week building barriers. Upstream, Odessa was threatened by a strained dam holding back the rising Big Stone Lake.
Many bridges across the region were closed because of rising rivers. Authorities in Stillwater, Minnesota, tried to weigh down a bridge to prevent the rushing St. Croix River from washing it away.
"Everybody has pitched in and helped out," Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson told CNN. "We anticipate that we're not going to be through this for another five weeks."

The storm that paralysed the northern plains also spun into Canada, closing key highways and cancelling flights for 2,000 stranded passengers at Winnipeg's airport. Hundreds of cars were abandoned in and around Winnipeg but only a few injuries were reported.
